tagline: A letter from prison about God's plan to gather all things in Christ, and about the one new people, Jew and Gentile together, that his grace has made.
overview:
Ephesians is a letter in two halves. The first three chapters are praise, prayer, and teaching: God chose a people in Christ before the world began, raised them from spiritual death by grace alone, and in the cross tore down the wall that divided Jews from Gentiles, so that the two now make one body, one household, one temple where God lives by his Spirit. The last three chapters turn that teaching into life: walk worthy of this calling, keep the unity the Spirit has made, put off the old self and put on the new, live out the gospel in marriage, family, and work, and stand firm against the spiritual powers of evil in the armor God supplies.

The letter has little of the controversy that drives Galatians or Corinthians. There is no false teacher to answer and no named crisis. Instead it steps back and looks at the whole of what God is doing, a plan that reaches from before the foundation of the world to the fullness of time, when he will bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ (1:10). The church is at the center of that picture, not as an institution but as the first sign of a reconciled creation.

Few books have shaped Christian thinking about grace and the church as much as this one. Its summary of salvation, “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (2:8-9), became a touchstone of the Reformation. Its household instructions (5:21-6:9) remain some of the most debated verses in the New Testament, both for what they say about marriage and for how they were later used to defend slavery.
author:
The letter names Paul as its author twice (1:1 and 3:1), and the early church received it as his without question. It is well attested among second-century Christian writers, and until the modern period almost no one doubted it.

Since the nineteenth century many scholars have argued that it was written after Paul's death by a follower writing in his name, a practice (called pseudonymity) that some think was an accepted way to carry a teacher's thought forward. Their reasons are these: the Greek style is unlike the letters nearly everyone accepts as Paul's, with very long sentences (1:3-14 is a single sentence in Greek); the vocabulary and emphases differ, with salvation spoken of as already completed (2:5-8) and the church as universal rather than local; the apostles and prophets are described as the church's foundation (2:20), which reads to some like a later generation looking back; the letter closely parallels Colossians, as if one were built from the other; and it sounds impersonal for a man who spent more than two years in Ephesus (1:15 and 3:2 speak as if Paul and the readers knew each other only by report).

Many other scholars defend Paul's authorship. Style varies with subject, and a letter of praise and prayer will read differently from a letter of argument. Paul commonly used a secretary, which could account for differences in wording. The overlap with Colossians fits one writer composing two letters at about the same time and sending both with Tychicus (6:21-22; Colossians 4:7-8). The impersonal tone is explained if the letter was meant for several churches, not Ephesus alone. And the early church, which did reject some writings as falsely attributed, accepted this one. Both positions are held by careful, faithful scholars; readers on both sides agree the letter carries Paul's gospel.
date: If Paul wrote it, he did so as a prisoner (3:1; 4:1; 6:20), most likely during his house arrest in Rome, traditionally dated around AD 60 to 62, at about the same time as Colossians and Philemon. Some who accept Paul's authorship place it during an earlier imprisonment, in Caesarea around AD 57 to 59 or possibly in Ephesus in the mid-50s. Scholars who think a later follower wrote it usually date it between about AD 80 and 100. It must be earlier than the early second century, when Christian writers already appear to know it.
setting:
Ephesus was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire, a port on the western coast of what is now Turkey and the leading city of the Roman province of Asia. It was famous for its temple of Artemis, counted among the wonders of the ancient world, and for its trade in magic and religious objects. Acts 19 tells how Paul spent more than two years there, teaching daily in a lecture hall, how books of magic worth a great sum were burned by new believers, and how a riot broke out when silversmiths who made shrines of Artemis saw their trade threatened. From Ephesus the gospel spread through the surrounding province.

There is a textual question in the letter's first verse. The words “in Ephesus” (1:1) are missing from the earliest surviving manuscripts, including a papyrus from about AD 200 and the two great fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus in their original form. The second-century teacher Marcion knew the letter under the title To the Laodiceans. For these reasons many scholars think the letter was a circular, meant to be carried from church to church in the province of Asia, with Ephesus as its best-known destination; some connect it with the letter from Laodicea mentioned in Colossians 4:16. Others think the words are original and were dropped in some copies. Either way, the readers were mostly Gentile believers (2:11; 3:1) in the cities of western Asia Minor, living among temples, guilds, and household religion, and needing to understand who they now were.
purpose: Ephesians is written to Gentile Christians to tell them who they are in Christ and how to live as that people. It aims to deepen their grasp of God's grace and power (1:15-23; 3:14-21), to show them that they have been joined to Israel's hope and to Jewish believers as one body (2:11-3:13), and to teach them to live out that unity in ordinary life: in speech, sexuality, work, marriage, parenting, and the household. Its closing call to stand in God's armor (6:10-20) reminds readers living in a city full of spiritual rivals that the church's struggle is not finally with people but with the powers of evil, and that Christ has already been seated far above them (1:20-21).
story: Ephesians looks back to the promises God made to Abraham and to Israel, the covenants of the promise from which Gentiles were once strangers (2:12), and announces that in Christ those promises now include the nations. It stands after the events of Acts, reflecting a church that has become mostly Gentile and that must learn to be one people with Jewish believers. Among Paul's letters it belongs with Colossians, Philemon, and Philippians as the Prison Letters. Its vision reaches forward to the end of the story, when all things in heaven and on earth are brought together in Christ (1:10), the same horizon Revelation paints as a new heaven and a new earth.
christ: Christ is the center of everything in Ephesians. The phrase “in Christ” and its equivalents run through the letter: every blessing, the choosing, the redemption, the forgiveness, and the sealing with the Spirit happen “in Him” (1:3-14). God raised Christ from the dead and seated him above every power in the heavenly realms, and made him head over all things for the church, which is his body (1:20-23). By his blood and in his flesh he made peace between Jew and Gentile and between both and God (2:13-18). He ascended and gave gifts to his people (4:7-11), and his self-giving love for the church is the pattern for marriage (5:25). The letter also shows the Father, Son, and Spirit working together in salvation, which later Christians recognized as a witness to the Trinity.
reading: Read Ephesians slowly and read it whole. The long sentences of the opening chapters are prayer and praise, not tangled argument, and they are best read aloud. Watch for the hinge at 4:1, where teaching turns to instruction with the word “then”: the letter's commands grow out of what God has already done, and cutting them off from chapters 1 to 3 turns grace into moralism. Watch the key words: grace, in Christ, mystery, body, walk, and the heavenly realms. The household instructions (5:21-6:9) should be read against the Roman household of the first century, whose structure Paul did not invent, and with attention to how he reshapes it, opening with a call to submit to one another (5:21, read by some as mutual submission among all believers and by others as submission within ordered relationships) and holding the powerful to account before Christ. A common misreading treats the letter's language of choosing and predestination as abstract speculation; in context it is praise, meant to give believers confidence and humility.

structure.title: Greeting and blessing
structure.summary: Paul greets the saints and praises the Father for every spiritual blessing in Christ: chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, and sealed with the Spirit.

structure.title: A prayer for understanding
structure.summary: Paul prays that readers will know their hope, their inheritance, and the power that raised Christ and seated him over every rule and authority.

structure.title: Saved by grace, made one
structure.summary: Dead in sin, believers are made alive with Christ by grace through faith; Gentiles once far away are brought near, and Jew and Gentile become one new humanity and one temple.

structure.title: The mystery revealed and a second prayer
structure.summary: Paul explains his calling to make known the mystery that Gentiles are fellow heirs, then prays that readers will grasp the immeasurable love of Christ.

structure.title: Walking worthy of the calling
structure.summary: Keep the unity of the Spirit, use Christ's gifts to build up the body, put off the old self and put on the new, and walk in love, light, and wisdom.

structure.title: The Christian household
structure.summary: Mutual submission shapes the relationships of wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters, all under the one Lord.

structure.title: The armor of God and farewell
structure.summary: Believers stand against the spiritual forces of evil in God's armor and pray; Paul commends Tychicus and closes with peace and grace.

themes.title: Grace
themes.body: Salvation in Ephesians is God's work from first to last. God chose, God predestined, God lavished grace, God made the dead alive. Human beings contribute nothing but the need; even faith is the way the gift is received, not a work that earns it. Yet believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works that God prepared in advance (2:10).

themes.title: One new humanity
themes.body: The deepest division of Paul's world, between Jew and Gentile, has been overcome in the cross. Christ has torn down the dividing wall of hostility and made the two into one new man (2:14-15). This is not a side topic but the heart of the mystery Paul was given to preach (3:6). The church is meant to be a visible display, even to the powers in the heavenly realms, that God can make one people out of enemies (3:10).

themes.title: The church as body, temple, and bride
themes.body: Ephesians gives the church three great pictures. It is the body of Christ, with Christ as its head, growing as each part does its work (4:15-16). It is a holy temple, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, where God dwells by the Spirit (2:20-22). And it is the bride whom Christ loved and gave himself up for, to make her holy (5:25-27). Each picture presents the church as more than a voluntary club.

themes.title: The powers
themes.body: Ephesians speaks more than any other of Paul's letters about rulers, authorities, and powers in the heavenly realms. Christ has been seated far above them all (1:21), the church makes God's wisdom known to them (3:10), and believers struggle not against flesh and blood but against them (6:12). The letter takes spiritual evil seriously without making it the center: the center is Christ's victory, and the believer's task is to stand.

themes.title: A worthy walk
themes.body: The verb “walk” marks the letter's practical half: walk worthy of the calling (4:1), no longer as the Gentiles walk (4:17), walk in love (5:2), walk as children of light (5:8), walk wisely (5:15). Christian life is described as a way of walking, a whole manner of conduct, shaped by the new identity God has given rather than by rules alone.

keyChapters.why: One of the great passages of praise in the Bible, setting out God's plan to bring all things together in Christ and the blessings believers receive in him.
The classic statement of salvation by grace through faith, followed by the reconciliation of Jew and Gentile into one new humanity through the cross.
The turn from teaching to life: the unity of the Spirit, the gifts of the ascended Christ to build up the body, and the call to put on the new self.
Contains the most debated passage on Christian marriage, which ties husband and wife to the relationship between Christ and the church.
Closes the household instructions with children, parents, slaves, and masters, and gives the well-known picture of the armor of God.

parts.body:
Ephesians is a letter. It names Paul as its writer, written from prison to believers in Ephesus and the cities around it, in what is now western Turkey. It has 6 chapters and can be read aloud in about twenty minutes.

Galatians, just before it in the Bible, is a letter written in a fight. Ephesians is calmer. It reads like a prayer that becomes teaching. Its first three chapters praise God for what he has done. Its last three show how to live because of it.

The letter's great theme is God's plan, kept hidden for ages and now made known: “to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ” (1:10). God is gathering a broken world back under one head. And he has already begun, by making one new people out of Jews and Gentiles, people who had been divided by a wall of hostility. “For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one” (2:14).

At the centre is grace. The readers were once “dead in your trespasses and sins” (2:1). God made them alive. “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (2:8).

Then comes the turn. “I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received” (4:1). The rest of the letter is that walk: unity, truth-telling, kindness, forgiveness, a new way of speaking, of working, of loving at home, and of standing firm against evil.

Some of the most loved prayers in the Bible are here. Paul prays that his readers may know “the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ” (3:18-19). The letter is short. Its view is as wide as heaven and earth.

The letter names its writer twice: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (1:1), and “I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus” (3:1). The early church received it as Paul's without question, and Christian writers of the second century already knew it. For most of the church's history almost no one doubted that Paul wrote it.

Since the 1800s many scholars have argued that a follower of Paul wrote it after his death, in Paul's name, to carry his teaching forward. Here are their reasons, put as they would put them. The Greek style is unlike the letters nearly everyone accepts as Paul's, with very long sentences: 1:3-14 is one sentence in Greek. Some words and ideas differ, such as salvation spoken of as already complete (2:5-8), and ‘the church’ meaning the whole church in the world more than a local gathering. The apostles and prophets are called the church's foundation (2:20), which reads to some like a later generation looking back. The letter is close to Colossians, as if one were built from the other. And it sounds strangely distant for a man who spent more than two years in Ephesus.

Many other scholars hold that Paul wrote it. Here are their reasons, as they would put them. Style changes with subject, and a letter of praise and prayer will read differently from a letter of argument. Paul used secretaries, which could explain differences in wording. The likeness to Colossians fits one writer sending two letters at the same time by the same messenger, Tychicus (6:21-22; Colossians 4:7-8). The distant tone fits a letter meant for several churches, not Ephesus alone, as the next part explains. And the early church, which did reject some writings that falsely claimed an apostle's name, accepted this one.

These notes do not choose. Both views are held by careful and faithful scholars. The church has received Ephesians as Scripture from the beginning, and readers on both sides agree that it carries Paul's gospel. These notes speak of the writer as Paul, as the letter does.

Ephesus was one of the great cities of the Roman world. It was a port near the west coast of what is now Turkey, and the leading city of the Roman province of Asia. Its temple of the goddess Artemis was counted among the wonders of the ancient world. Acts tells how Paul stayed in Ephesus more than two years, teaching every day; how new believers burned their books of magic; and how silversmiths who made little shrines of Artemis started a riot when their trade was threatened (Acts 19).

The letter's first verse raises a question. In the BSB it reads, “To the saints in Ephesus” (1:1). But the words ‘in Ephesus’ are missing from three of the earliest copies that survive: a papyrus copy from about AD 200, and the two great books of the 300s called Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, as first written. And Marcion, a teacher of the second century whose views the church rejected, knew the letter by the title ‘To the Laodiceans’.

So many scholars think Ephesians was a circular letter, meant to be carried from church to church in the province of Asia, with Ephesus, the chief city, as its best-known stop. Some link it with the letter ‘from Laodicea’ that Paul mentions in Colossians 4:16. Others think the words ‘in Ephesus’ are original and were left out in some copies, and they note that every early translation of the letter has them. These notes do not choose.

Either way, the readers were mostly Gentile believers (2:11; 3:1) in the cities of western Asia Minor. They lived among temples, magic, trade guilds and household gods. They needed to know who they now were.

The writer is in prison. He calls himself “the prisoner of Christ Jesus” (3:1) and “an ambassador in chains” (6:20). He sends the letter by Tychicus, who will tell them how he is (6:21-22).

If Paul wrote it, most think he wrote from Rome, where Acts says he lived under guard for two years, about AD 60 to 62 (Acts 28:30). On this view Ephesians was written at about the same time as Colossians and Philemon, which name the same messenger. Some who hold that Paul wrote it place it in an earlier imprisonment, at Caesarea (Acts 23 to 26), or at Ephesus itself.

Scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote it usually date it later, between about AD 80 and 100. All agree that it was written before the early 100s, when Christian writers already seem to know it.

These notes do not choose. The prison matters more than the year. A man in chains writes a letter full of praise, and asks his readers to pray that he will speak boldly (6:19-20).

Ephesians falls into two halves, joined at 4:1.

Chapters 1 to 3: what God has done. After a short greeting, Paul bursts into praise (1:3-14): God has blessed us in Christ, chose us, adopted us, redeemed us, made known his plan, and sealed us with the Spirit. He prays that his readers will know the hope, the riches and the power God has given (1:15-23). Then he tells the story of grace: dead in sin, made alive with Christ (2:1-10). Gentiles once far off have been brought near, and Jews and Gentiles have become one new people, one household, one temple (2:11-22). Paul explains his own calling to make known this ‘mystery’ (3:1-13), and prays again, for strength and for love beyond knowing (3:14-21). The first half ends in praise: “Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine” (3:20).

Chapters 4 to 6: how to live. “As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received” (4:1). Keep the unity of the Spirit; grow up together through the gifts Christ gives (4:1-16). Put off the old life and put on the new: tell the truth, deal with anger, work honestly, speak kindly, forgive (4:17-32). Walk in love, in light, and in wisdom (5:1-20). Then the household: wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters (5:21 to 6:9). Last, stand firm in the armour of God, and pray (6:10-20). A short farewell closes the letter.

The word ‘walk’ runs through the second half: walk worthy (4:1), walk in love (5:2), walk as children of light (5:8), walk wisely (5:15). The commands grow out of the gifts. Cut chapters 4 to 6 off from chapters 1 to 3, and grace becomes a list of rules.

Grace. Salvation is God's gift from first to last. He chose, he loved, he made alive, he raised and seated us with Christ. “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith” (2:8), and the church confesses this not as a view but as the faith: salvation is God's own act, through the cross, received as a gift.

In Christ. The phrase ‘in Christ’, or ‘in Him’, comes again and again, especially in chapter 1. Every blessing is found in him. Believers are joined to him, so that what is true of him becomes true of them: raised, seated, loved.

One new people. The deepest division in Paul's world, as a Jew saw it, was between Israel and the nations. Ephesians says Christ has torn down the wall between them and made “one new man out of the two” (2:15). Gentiles are “fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise” (3:6). The church is meant to show the world what God's peace looks like.

The church. Ephesians calls the church Christ's body (1:23), God's household and temple (2:19-22), and the bride Christ loves (5:25-27). The church is not a club of the like-minded. It is God's new family, and through it God makes his wisdom known even to the powers of heaven (3:10).

The powers. The letter speaks often of ‘rulers and authorities’ and ‘the heavenly realms’. Its readers lived in a city famous for magic and fear of spirits. Ephesians says Christ is seated “far above all rule and authority” (1:21). Believers stand against evil, but not alone, and not with the weapons of this world.

The Trinity. Again and again the letter speaks of the Father, the Son and the Spirit working together: chosen by the Father, redeemed by the Son, sealed by the Spirit (1:3-14); access “to the Father by one Spirit” through Christ (2:18); one Spirit, one Lord, one God and Father of all (4:4-6). The church confesses one God in three persons, and Ephesians shows that faith already at work in prayer and praise.

Ephesians quotes the Old Testament less than Galatians or Romans, but its mind is full of Israel's Scriptures.

It reads Psalm 110, where God says to the king, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (Psalm 110:1), and Psalm 8, “You made him ruler of the works of Your hands; You have placed everything under his feet” (Psalm 8:6), as fulfilled when God raised Christ and seated him at his right hand (1:20-22).

It hears Isaiah's promise of peace “to those far and near” (Isaiah 57:19) in the coming of Christ to Gentiles and Jews (2:17). It reads Psalm 68:18, a song of God going up in victory, as a picture of Christ ascending and giving gifts (4:8). It quotes Zechariah on speaking the truth to one another (4:25), and a psalm on being angry without sinning (4:26; Psalm 4:4). It quotes Genesis 2:24 on a man and his wife becoming one flesh (5:31), and the commandment to honour father and mother (6:2-3). And its armour of God is taken from Isaiah, where God himself puts on righteousness and salvation to save his people (Isaiah 59:17).

Where Paul's wording differs from the Old Testament in the Berean Standard Bible, it is often because he follows the old Greek translation, while the BSB translates the Hebrew. The chapter notes point this out where it happens.

Behind the whole letter stands the promise to Abraham, that all nations would be blessed through him. Ephesians says that promise has now come true: Gentiles who were “strangers to the covenants of the promise” (2:12) are now members of God's household.

parts.h: ‘Chosen in Him’: how Christians read it
parts.body:
Ephesians opens with words about God choosing: “For He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world” (1:4), and “He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ” (1:5). Christians have long read these words in different ways. The note on 1:3-14 sets out the readings; here is the short form.

Reformed Christians read them as God's loving choice, before creation, of particular people for salvation, resting wholly on his free mercy. Arminian and Wesleyan Christians read them as God's choice of all who are in Christ, with God knowing beforehand who would freely trust him. Others, in both traditions, stress that Paul speaks of ‘us’, a people chosen ‘in Him’, and that each person comes into that chosen people by faith. These notes do not choose, as the notes on Romans 8 and 9 do not.

What all agree on is the reason the words are there. They are praise, not a puzzle. Paul does not write them to make anyone anxious about whether they are chosen. He writes them so that believers will know their salvation began in God's love, not in their own effort, and so that no one can boast.

Ephesians 5:21 to 6:9 speaks to wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters. These are some of the most debated verses in the New Testament, and the chapter notes take each one with care. Here is the shape.

Paul did not invent the household he speaks to. In the Roman world, writers had long described the household as ruled by its male head, over wife, children and slaves. Paul speaks to that household as it was. But he changes it in three ways. He speaks to the weaker members first, as people who can choose and who answer to Christ. He speaks to the stronger members with demands, not privileges: husbands are to love as Christ gave himself, fathers are not to provoke, masters are to remember that they too have a Master in heaven. And he puts the whole household under Christ.

Churches today read these verses differently, especially on marriage. All agree that they call for mutual love, that Christ's self-giving is the pattern, and that they give no one a licence to control or harm another. Where churches differ, and how, the note on 5:21-33 sets out, without taking a side.

The words to slaves were misused for centuries to defend slavery. That misuse was wrong. The note on 6:5-9 says what the text said to its first hearers, and how it was turned against them.

It is not a letter against the Jewish people. Its great theme is that Gentiles have been brought into Israel's hope, made “fellow citizens with the saints” (2:19). The wall Christ tore down was the hostility between peoples, not the Jewish people themselves. Any reading that turns this letter into contempt for Jews has turned it upside down. The note on Acts 2:22-28 says why this site rejects such readings.

It is not a licence for control at home. The household passages are among the most misused in the Bible. Nothing in them tells anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger, and nothing in them gives anyone the right to rule another by fear.

It is not a call to fight people. The armour of God is for standing firm against evil, “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (6:12). Its weapons are truth, righteousness, peace, faith, salvation, the word of God and prayer. It gives no one a reason to treat neighbours, opponents or other nations as enemies to be defeated, and the cross belongs to no flag.

It is not a promise of wealth. ‘The riches of His grace’ (1:7) are riches of mercy, not money. Any teaching that turns God's blessings in Christ into a promise of health and wealth misreads the letter of a man writing in chains.

And it is not abstract. Ephesians is sometimes read as lofty and far from ordinary life. But its second half is about how you speak, how you handle anger, how you work, how you treat your family, and whether you forgive. Its view is as wide as heaven, and its feet are on the ground.

Read it in one sitting, aloud if you can. The long sentences of chapter 1 are praise, and they are easier to follow spoken than read silently. Let them carry you.

Notice the hinge at 4:1. Everything before it is what God has done. Everything after it is how to live because of it. Do not read the commands without the gifts.

Notice the prayers. Paul prays twice (1:15-23; 3:14-21), and asks for prayer at the end (6:18-20). The letter is meant to be prayed as well as studied. Try praying Paul's prayers for someone you love.

Notice the words that come back: grace, in Christ, mystery, body, walk, love, the heavenly realms.

When you reach the household passages, read them slowly, in their setting, and read the notes on them. Remember that the same letter says, “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:21).

And let the letter read you. It asks whether you know how much you are loved. It asks whether the walls you live behind, of race, class, politics or pride, are walls Christ has already torn down. It asks how you speak at home and at work. And it ends where it began, with grace.

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘To the saints in Ephesus.’ Why some early copies leave out ‘in Ephesus’, and what that may say about the letter.
Chosen and predestined in Christ. How Reformed and Arminian or Wesleyan Christians read these words, and why they are written as praise.
‘By grace you have been saved through faith … not by works.’ Grace, faith and the good works God prepared.
The dividing wall torn down. What wall, what ‘abolishing’ the law means, and why it is no word against the Jewish people.
‘He also descended to the lower parts of the earth.’ The incarnation, the grave, or the realm of the dead.
Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers. Whether some of these gifts have ceased, and how churches differ.
‘Be angry, yet do not sin.’ What to do with anger, and what this verse does not ask of someone who has been wronged.
Wives and husbands. What all agree on, the complementarian and egalitarian readings, and why this passage never tells anyone to stay in danger.
Slaves and masters. What the text said to its first hearers, how it was misused to defend slavery, and why that was wrong.
The armour of God. A struggle not against flesh and blood, and why it is no licence for aggression toward anyone.

words.line: Greek charis, God's free gift and the goodwill behind it. “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith” (2:8).
Joined to Christ, sharing his life. The phrase, with ‘in Him’, runs all through chapter 1: every blessing is found there (1:3).
God's choosing and his deciding beforehand (1:4-5, 11). Christians read these words in more than one way; see the part above.
Greek mystērion, a secret once hidden and now made known by God: that Gentiles are “fellow heirs” with Israel in Christ (3:6).
The unseen world where Christ reigns and where the powers of evil still act (1:3, 20; 6:12).
Spiritual powers opposed to God. Christ is seated far above them (1:21), and the church makes God's wisdom known to them (3:10).
The church as Christ's body, many members with one head (1:22-23; 4:15-16).
Not only calm, but enemies made friends. Christ “is our peace” (2:14), making Jews and Gentiles one.
Paul's word for how a person lives day by day. “walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received” (4:1).
The life before Christ and the life made new in him, put off and put on like clothes (4:22-24).
Greek hypotassō, to place oneself under, to defer. Asked first of all believers toward one another (5:21).
Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer (6:13-18), taken from Isaiah's picture of God himself.

timeline.what: Paul in Ephesus more than two years, teaching daily; books of magic burned; the riot of the silversmiths (Acts 19).
Paul says farewell to the elders of the Ephesian church at Miletus (Acts 20:17-38).
Paul is held at Caesarea under two Roman governors (Acts 23 to 26). Some place the letter here.
Paul under guard in Rome for two years (Acts 28:30). Most who hold that Paul wrote Ephesians place it here, with Colossians and Philemon.
When scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote the letter usually date it.
Christian writers already know the letter. Marcion knows it as ‘To the Laodiceans’.
A papyrus copy of Paul's letters, among the earliest that survive, has the letter without the words ‘in Ephesus’.
The great books Sinaiticus and Vaticanus copy the letter, also without ‘in Ephesus’ as first written.

map.title: Ephesus, the cities of Asia, and the places of Paul's imprisonment

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: The leading city of the province of Asia, with its great temple of Artemis, where Paul taught for more than two years (Acts 19). The letter bears its name, though some early copies leave it out (1:1).

places.name: Laodicea
places.line: A city of the Lycus valley, east of Ephesus. Marcion knew this letter as ‘To the Laodiceans’, and some link it with the letter ‘from Laodicea’ of Colossians 4:16.

places.name: Caesarea
places.line: Where Paul was held for two years before he was sent to Rome (Acts 23 to 26). Some think he wrote the letter here, as ‘an ambassador in chains’ (6:20).

places.name: Rome
places.line: Where Paul lived under guard for two years (Acts 28:30). Most who hold that Paul wrote the letter think he wrote it here, as ‘the prisoner of Christ Jesus’ (3:1).

teaching.mapNote: The letter went to Ephesus and very likely to other churches of the province of Asia, such as Laodicea. It was written from prison: most often thought Rome, by some Caesarea, by a few Ephesus itself.
